'''Stephen James Benkovic''' is an American chemist known for his contributions to the field of [[Enzyme|enzymology]]. He holds the Evan Pugh University Professorship and Eberly Chair in [[Chemistry]] at [[Pennsylvania State University|The Pennsylvania State University.]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=sjb1 |url=https://science.psu.edu/chem/people/sjb1 |access-date=2023-07-04 |website=science.psu.edu |language=en}}</ref> He has developed [[boron compounds]] that are active [[pharmacophore]]s against a variety of diseases. Benkovic has concentrated on the assembly and kinetic attributes of the enzymatic machinery that performs [[DNA replication]], [[DNA repair]], and [[Purine metabolism|purine biosynthesis]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Benkovic Laboratory – |url=https://sites.psu.edu/benkoviclab/ |access-date=2023-07-04 |website=sites.psu.edu}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=toddviola |date=2014-01-15 |title=Stephen J. Benkovic |url=https://www.fi.edu/en/laureates/stephen-j-benkovic |access-date=2023-07-04 |website=The Franklin Institute |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Stephen Benkovic, Ph.D. |url=https://boundlessbio.com/who-we-are/stephen-j-benkovic-ph-d/ |access-date=2023-07-04 |website=Boundless Bio |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Education ==
Benkovic was born in [[Orange, New Jersey|Orange, New Jersey, US]]. He attended [[Lehigh University]], where he received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in [[chemistry]] and A.B. degree in [[English literature]] in 1960.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Stephen Benkovic |url=https://sites.psu.edu/benkoviclab/stephen-benkovic/ |access-date=2023-07-04 |website=sites.psu.edu}}</ref> He then earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in [[organic chemistry]] from [[Cornell University]] in 1963.<ref name=":1" /> He was a postdoctoral research associate at the [[University of California]] at [[Santa Barbara, California|Santa Barbara]] from 1964 to 1965.

In 1965, he became a member of the Chemistry Department at [[Pennsylvania State University|Penn State University]], and later in 1970, he was promoted to the position of full professor of chemistry.<ref name=":1" /> He received further recognition in 1977 as an Evan Pugh Professor of Chemistry and in 1988 as the holder of the Eberly Chair in Chemistry.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Benkovic has made contributions that have impacted our understanding of [[biological process]]es. He was among the first to hypothesize that conformational changes outside an enzyme's active site were necessary for achieving maximal [[catalysis]].<ref name=":9" /> This was illustrated in his studies on [[Dihydrofolate reductase|dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)]] that identified dynamic structural changes and their time scale that optimized the enzyme turnover.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cameron |first1=C. '''Conformational Movements'''

A major theme of Benkovic's research has been understanding the source of the efficiency of enzymatic catalysis.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Benkovic |first1=Stephen J. |last2=Hammes-Schiffer |first2=Sharon |date=2003-08-29 |title=A perspective on enzyme catalysis |journal=Science |volume=301 |issue=5637 |pages=1196–1202 |doi=10.1126/science.1085515 |issn=1095-9203 |pmid=12947189|bibcode=2003Sci...301.1196B |s2cid=7899320 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bruice |first1=Thomas C. |last2=Benkovic |first2=Stephen J. |date=2000-05-01 |title=Chemical Basis for Enzyme Catalysis |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/bi0003689 |journal=Biochemistry |language=en |volume=39 |issue=21 |pages=6267–6274 |doi=10.1021/bi0003689 |pmid=10828939 |issn=0006-2960|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He first dissected into individual steps the catalytic cycle used by [[Dihydrofolate reductase|dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)]] using pre-steady-state methods and then tied the contribution of various [[amino acid]]s, both within and outside the active site, to specific steps.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":16" /> Significant changes in the rates of hydride transfer were not limited to active-site residues, nor were the effects of multiple mutations additive in terms of free energy. The amide backbone and side chains of these distal residues were found by NMR to be in regions of high frequency motion (n-psec) and by molecular dynamic simulations the motions of these distal residues were found to be coupled.<ref name=":12" /> Genomic analysis of multiple DHFR sequences revealed low overall [[DNA sequencing|DNA sequence homology]] (30%), but surprisingly high conservation in the same regions whose [[amino acid]]s had been implicated in catalysis by kinetic analysis, NMR measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations.<ref name=":9" /> The latter directly incorporated these distal residues into a network that acted along the reaction coordinate to facilitate the hydride transfer.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":13" />[[File:NADPH image.png|thumb|Illustration]]
This concept was further elaborated to posit that the measured rates of steps that constitute the turnover cycle of DHFR represent the rates of the conformational changes required to execute the chemical transformation.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Hammes-Schiffer |first1=Sharon |last2=Benkovic |first2=Stephen J. |date=2006-06-01 |title=Relating Protein Motion to Catalysis |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.biochem.75.103004.142800 |journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry |language=en |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=519–541 |doi=10.1146/annurev.biochem.75.103004.142800 |pmid=16756501 |bibcode=2006ARBio..75..519H |issn=0066-4154|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The enzymic reaction is not limited by the energetics of the chemical reaction but by the mechanics of sampling that occur within the enzyme substrate complex.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hammes |first1=Gordon G. |last2=Benkovic |first2=Stephen J. |last3=Hammes-Schiffer |first3=Sharon |date=2011-12-06 |title=Flexibility, diversity, and cooperativity: pillars of enzyme catalysis |journal=Biochemistry |volume=50 |issue=48 |pages=10422–10430 |doi=10.1021/bi201486f |issn=1520-4995 |pmc=3226911 |pmid=22029278}}</ref>

This concept of biological catalysis has the enzyme's highly pre-organized [[Michaelis–Menten kinetics|Michaelis complex]] with its active-site residues and substrates juxtaposed by using the dynamics of the protein fold to sample substrate and active site conformations in order to find those optimal for the chemical transformation. The actual chemistry of bond breaking and forming is fast relative to the sampling process. Only a small change triggered by movement within the protein fold along a network of coupled residues is needed to surmount the reaction barrier.<ref name=":4" /> The protein fold dictates the type of chemistry that a class of enzymes can accomplish (a rationale for the common mechanistic element extent in protein super-families); allosteric effects are a consequence of creating or inhibiting such networks and drugs can be designed that target such networks.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Goodey |first1=Nina M. |last2=Benkovic |first2=Stephen J. |date=2008-08-01 |title=Allosteric regulation and catalysis emerge via a common route |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |volume=4 |issue=8 |pages=474–482 |doi=10.1038/nchembio.98 |issn=1552-4469 |pmid=18641628}}</ref><ref name=":17" /> It also explains the generally low catalytic activity of more rigid structures such as [[macrocycle]]s and [[Antibody|antibodies]].<ref name=":18" />

'''A multi-enzyme complex for the replication of DNA—the T4 replisome'''

Of particular importance is how multiple protein systems such as the [[replisome]]s responsible for [[DNA replication]] function where [[Protein–protein interaction|protein-protein interactions]] create a large catalytic network. The T4 replisome can be assembled in vitro from eight separate proteins into the four units that catalyze leading and lagging strand synthesis at a replication fork.<ref name=":5" /> With a functioning replisome capable of leading/lagging strand synthesis in hand, key discoveries of broad interest applicable to other replisomes were made. Firstly the [[polymerase]] actively exchanges in/out of the two [[Enzyme|holoenzymes]] within the [[replisome]] thus providing a  "remodeling" flexibility for the repair of stalled replication forks that occur on damaged DNA strands by other lesion bypass [[polymerase]]s.<ref name=":23" /> Secondly, two mechanisms dictate [[Okazaki fragments|Okazaki fragment]] length: the classical collision mechanism where a finished Okazaki fragment abuts the previous one releasing the lagging strand polymerase and the signaling mechanism where the lagging strand polymerase recycles before the completion of the previous Okazaki fragment.<ref name=":5" /> This feature is essential to maintain coordinated leading/lagging strand synthesis.<ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Jingsong |last2=Trakselis |first2=Michael A. |last3=Roccasecca |first3=Rosa Maria |last4=Benkovic |first4=Stephen J. |date=2003-12-12 |title=The Application of a Minicircle Substrate in the Study of the Coordinated T4 DNA Replication* |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |language=en |volume=278 |issue=50 |pages=49828–49838 |doi=10.1074/jbc.M307406200 |issn=0021-9258|doi-access=free |pmid=14500718 }}</ref>
[[File:FGMAS GART and MERGE.png|thumb|FGMAS GART]]
'''''De Novo'' Purine Biosynthesis by a Purinosome Metabolon'''
[[File:De Novo Purine Biosynthesis.png|thumb|De Novo Purine Biosynthesis]]
A longstanding question in [[Metabolism|cellular metabolism]] is how metabolic enzymes in a given network organize within the [[cytosol]], densely packed with myriad proteins and [[metabolite]]s, to facilitate [[Flux (metabolism)|metabolic flux]]. One solution is through the formation of a [[macromolecular assembly|macromolecular complex]] of enzymes, termed a '[[metabolon]]'.<ref name=":14" /> The ''de novo'' purine biosynthetic pathway is a highly conserved, energy-intensive pathway that generates inosine 5ᶦ-monophosphate (IMP) from [[Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate|phosphoribosylpyrophosphate (PRPP)]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pareek |first1=Vidhi |last2=Pedley |first2=Anthony M. |last3=Benkovic |first3=Stephen J. |date=2021-02-01 |title=Human de novo Purine Biosynthesis |journal=Critical Reviews in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=1–16 |doi=10.1080/10409238.2020.1832438 |issn=1040-9238 |pmc=7869020 |pmid=33179964}}</ref> In humans, this metabolic transformation is carried out in ten steps by the sequential orchestration of the activities of the six enzymes.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Pedley |first1=Anthony M. |last2=Benkovic |first2=Stephen J. |date=2017-02-01 |title=A New View into the Regulation of Purine Metabolism – The Purinosome |journal=Trends in Biochemical Sciences |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=141–154 |doi=10.1016/j.tibs.2016.09.009 |issn=0968-0004 |pmc=5272809 |pmid=28029518}}</ref> Evidence that the enzymes might condense within cells to form the purinosome derived from confocal microscopy on [[HeLa|HeLa cells]] using chimeric constructs of these enzymes that revealed in common merged punctates for the six enzymes as illustrated for the two enzymes, FGAMS and GART.<ref name=":20" /><ref name=":21" /> Unlike more traditional static [[metabolon]]s, [[purinosome]] formation is a reversible process.<ref name=":14">{{Cite book |last1=Pedley |first1=Anthony M. |last2=Benkovic |first2=Stephen J. |title=Protein Complex Assembly |date=2018 |chapter=Detecting Purinosome Metabolon Formation with Fluorescence Microscopy |series=Methods in Molecular Biology |language=en |volume=1764 |pages=279–289 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-7759-8_17 |pmid=29605921|pmc=6396681 |isbn=978-1-4939-7758-1 }}</ref> Spatial control of purinosome assembly in HeLa cells was found to be [[microtubule]] assisted and to colocalize with [[Mitochondrion|mitochondria]] as shown by super resolution chemical imaging.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=Chung Yu |last2=Pedley |first2=Anthony M. |last3=Kim |first3=Doory |last4=Xia |first4=Chenglong |last5=Zhuang |first5=Xiaowei |last6=Benkovic |first6=Stephen J. |date=2018-12-18 |title=Microtubule-directed transport of purine metabolons drives their cytosolic transit to mitochondria |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=115 |issue=51 |pages=13009–13014 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1814042115 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=6304990 |pmid=30509995 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018PNAS..11513009C }}</ref>  D''e novo'' purine biosynthesis is likely most efficient when [[purinosome]]s are located near [[Mitochondrion|mitochondria]] to capture needed substrates exported from the mitochondria.<ref name=":22" />

'''Drug Inhibitors Contain Boron'''

Although boron containing compounds had been eschewed as drugs because of their general toxicity by [[Medicinal chemistry|pharmaceutical chemists]], the Benkovic Lab created a library of boron containing compounds that showed surprising antifungal activity in phenotypic screening of [[yeast]]. Their low systemic toxicity in laboratory animals led to the founding of [[Anacor Pharmaceuticals]] by Benkovic and [[Lucy Shapiro]] that developed and commercialized [[nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug]] for [[Pediatrics|pediatric]] and adult use.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last1=Rock |first1=Fernando L. |last2=Mao |first2=Weimin |last3=Yaremchuk |first3=Anya |last4=Tukalo |first4=Mikhail |last5=Crépin |first5=Thibaut |last6=Zhou |first6=Huchen |last7=Zhang |first7=Yong-Kang |last8=Hernandez |first8=Vincent |last9=Akama |first9=Tsutomu |last10=Baker |first10=Stephen J. |last11=Plattner |first11=Jacob J. |last12=Shapiro |first12=Lucy |last13=Martinis |first13=Susan A. |last14=Benkovic |first14=Stephen J. |last15=Cusack |first15=Stephen |date=2007-06-22 |title=An antifungal agent inhibits an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase by trapping tRNA in the editing site |journal=Science |volume=316 |issue=5832 |pages=1759–1761 |doi=10.1126/science.1142189 |issn=1095-9203 |pmid=17588934|bibcode=2007Sci...316.1759R |s2cid=32667178 }}</ref> Continuing research suggests that [[boron]] containing molecules can have a potential to intervene in a variety of diseases such as—[[Infection|bacterial]] and [[fungal infection]]s, [[pulmonary hypertension]], and [[oncology]].
